analysis.one_liner: Shortens FDA monopoly protections for drugs whose makers raise prices sharply.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 6 Senate Democrats, sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a vote of any kind before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would penalize drug companies that raise prices sharply — more than 10% in one year, 18% in two, or 25% in three — by cutting short the exclusive right to sell the drug without generic competition, taking away 180 days plus more for each extra price bump [S3]. Companies that hike prices would have to report the increase to the government within 30 days, and could lose even more exclusivity time for failing to report [S3]. The Health and Human Services Secretary could waive the penalty if a company shows the price increase was needed to keep making the drug without hurting patient access [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, insurers, and government health programs that pay drug prices. When a drug's monopoly period is shortened, cheaper generic or biosimilar copies can reach the market sooner, which historically pushes prices down. The bill also gives the public a record of which manufacturers raised prices sharply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who buy drugs

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer that raises a drug's wholesale price more than 10% in one year, 18% in two years, or 25% in three years loses 180 days of market exclusivity, plus 30 more days for every 5-point increase past each threshold [S3].
Manufacturers must report qualifying price increases to HHS within 30 days or lose an additional 30 days of exclusivity per day late [S3].

The CRS summary describes the bill as directing the FDA to reduce market exclusivity when a manufacturer raises a drug's price by more than a specified percentage, waivable in certain circumstances [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers that raise prices sharply would lose some of the exclusive sales period that protects their revenue from generic competition. More broadly, companies would face a new reporting requirement and the risk of losing exclusivity on any drug they choose to hike.

drawbacks.text: Market exclusivity exists to reward drug development; shortening it for drugs with price increases could weaken the financial incentive to bring new medicines to market, which is why the bill includes a waiver process where the Secretary can lift the penalty if the price increase is necessary for production and does not restrict patient access [S3].

The penalty only reaches drugs that still hold FDA-granted exclusivity under the specified statutory provisions [S3]; older drugs that already lost their exclusivity could still be subject to large price increases with no penalty under this bill.
The remedy depends on generic competition arriving, and the bill does nothing to speed FDA review or remove other barriers that can delay generic entry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, well-documented problem — sudden large price increases on drugs protected by government-granted monopolies — with a targeted penalty rather than a broad price control, and it includes a waiver for cases where the increase is genuinely needed. Its main limits are that it only affects drugs that still hold exclusivity, and it works indirectly through future generic competition rather than lowering any price directly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the FLAT Prices Act in the Senate on February 6, 2019 [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The action history shows no committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or any further action after the referral for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill did not carry over [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they kept their full market exclusivity periods and faced no penalty or reporting requirement for raising prices. Patients paying for drugs saw no change from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where members stood, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill takes away 180 or more days of government-granted market exclusivity from any manufacturer that raises a drug's price past set thresholds, and imposes a reporting requirement. For the duration of exclusivity, a brand-name maker can charge prices without generic competition, so cutting that period short directly costs the industry revenue while lowering costs for patients and payers.
Shortened exclusivity periods mean generics and biosimilars can enter the market sooner after sharp price hikes, which is when generic makers can compete and prices tend to fall.
